description:
Pixel Payload: young game & software devs from Bursa. We're not here to ship a pile of code, we're here to build an experience: a story-driven game where players live a space mission, built on real NASA data.

We bring: game design, web dev, AI prototyping, storytelling.

Looking for: pixel artist/UI designer, sound designer, space science fans.

Think you could help us in any way? Don't be shy!
summary:
# Pixel Payload: People, Science, and Teamwork in Space Missions

**Pixel Payload** is a multiplayer space mission design game developed for the **Space Mission Design Game Challenge**, inspired by NASA’s approach to multidisciplinary teamwork in space missions.

In the game, each player takes on a different engineering role with specific responsibilities. While some roles require leadership and coordination, others focus on making informed decisions and taking responsibility within their own areas of expertise. No single role can complete the mission alone; every system and every decision is part of a much larger picture.

The main goal of the game is to combine scientific realism with entertainment while allowing players to experience teamwork, leadership, responsibility, and problem-solving firsthand. As the mission progresses, increasing difficulty, time pressure, unexpected challenges, and immediate feedback encourage players to stay calm under stress and make sound decisions.

Our game design draws inspiration from concepts such as **Flow Theory, intrinsic motivation, meaningful reward loops, and progressive difficulty**. This creates an experience in which players do more than simply design a space mission: they experience the importance of collaboration, witness the consequences of their decisions, and learn to manage a complex system together.
details:
PIXEL PAYLOAD is a multiplayer aerospace engineering platform that allows four players to connect via their web browsers—without the need for any software installation—to design, validate, and simulate a complete space mission, from the initial concept phase through to the launch operation. Participants join a session using a four-digit room code generated in the lobby and assume one of four specialized roles: Operator, Propulsion Engineer, Spacecraft Engineer, or Science & Payload Engineer. A "demo mode" is also available, enabling all four roles to be monitored from a single screen for presentations or reviews. The platform features two primary mission scenarios: a crewed lunar mission (inspired by the Artemis program) and a Mars rover mission (inspired by the Perseverance mission). Once a mission is selected, each player sees only the briefings and subsystems relevant to their specific role. In the crewed lunar mission, the team must operate within several constraints: a budget of 4,300 units, a maximum liftoff mass of 2,800 tons, a minimum liftoff thrust-to-weight ratio (TWR) of 1.2, and an HLS-style (Human Landing System) lander—launched separately—with a maximum mass of 42 tons. The Mars rover mission encompasses launch, a seven-month interplanetary cruise, atmospheric entry, descent and landing (EDL) via parachutes and powered descent, and the transmission of scientific data from the surface. The platform’s underlying physics engine incorporates the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation for multi-stage vehicles, power balance calculations, and atmospheric entry models. It calculates, in real-time, the budgets for launch, trans-lunar injection, lunar orbit insertion, the return journey, and surface landing and ascent. While engineers assemble components—such as main engines, fuel tanks, an Orion-inspired four-person crew capsule, Environmental Control and Life Support Systems (ECLSS), solar arrays, thermal control and radiation shielding, AxEMU-inspired EVA suits, and scientific instrumentation—the operator monitors all telemetry, initiates the pre-launch review, and executes the launch upon receiving confirmation from the team.

Through this architecture, users gain a hands-on understanding of real-world engineering, navigating the trade-offs between mass constraints, energy deficits, life-support consumables, and scientific mission objectives. Every piece of equipment in the catalog is labeled to distinguish between actual NASA engineering data and educational simplifications, ensuring transparency regarding the source of each estimate or game-mechanic assumption. The project’s primary goal is to transform the complex system engineering constraints of space missions—moving them beyond abstract formulas—into a collaborative STEM learning experience that can be easily implemented in schools, science centers, and workshops.

The application is built for standard computer hardware, utilizing HTML5, CSS3, modern JavaScript, and custom vector-based CAD/HUD interface components on the front end, while the back end employs Node.js, Express, and Socket.io to handle real-time multiplayer synchronization, role-based data filtering, and physics calculations. The project’s unique design approach integrates an asymmetric information structure with hierarchical communication protocols: engineers cannot view each other’s numerical data, nor can they send direct messages to one another. Parameters such as required payload mass, surface power, or data connectivity can only be requested through an operator. Furthermore, technical rules—dictated by the dependencies inherent to each piece of equipment (for instance, the requirement for life-support/ECLSS, flight computers, and crew-abort systems, inspired by the Orion capsule)—transform the assembly of components into a dynamic exercise in systems engineering verification. Our team has set out to maintain role-based data isolation on the server side, balance physical parameters derived from authentic NASA reports with fluid session pacing, and gamify both the engineering calculations and the hardware components themselves. Consequently, *Pixel Payload* was developed to allow anyone to experience a complete space mission—from the conceptual phase through to launch operations—directly addressing the issue where the complex trade-offs between budget, mass, power, propulsion, communications, and orbital constraints often remain purely abstract. By shifting away from passive knowledge transfer in space science and systems engineering education, this approach fosters a lasting learning impact: participants manage limited resources, engage in cross-team communication to reach collective decisions, and witness firsthand how every technical choice they make shapes the ultimate success of the mission.
